source.title: CiPO: Counterfactual Unlearning for Large Reasoning Models through Iterative Preference Optimization
source.authors: J. Li; Yong-Qiang Chen; Ning-Ning Ding

page_placements.theme: Forgetting metrics disagree: output-level forgetting while likelihood, ranks, CoT, paraphrase or facts still carry the target (no attack)

record.tranche_reason: Tests unlearning effectiveness and retained utility for LRMs using its own method and established baselines, but does not test whether post-unlearning attacks recover the knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper reports unlearning and utility metrics, but no recovery attack involving fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt changes. It discusses adversarial prompting as a possible residual risk, without reporting an attack result. Baseline comparisons beyond the rows below are omitted because the paper reports many results and the record prioritizes the principal method, original model, and selected comparison methods.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It proposes CiPO, an unlearning method for reasoning models, and reports its forgetting and utility scores against other unlearning baselines on R-TOFU and a RETURN-derived real-world set. It runs no recovery attack of any kind: no relearning fine-tune, no direction ablation or access analysis, no quantization, and no rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context probe. Its numbers say how much each method suppresses forget-set outputs on the standard prompts. They do not say whether that suppression is shallow or robust, so they cannot bear on whether Version A holds against simple attacks. The ethics section only notes that 'leakage may persist under adversarial prompting', with no result. Version A's 'near chance' part is also not measurable here: forget accuracy is open-ended LLM-judge accuracy with no chance level, and the forget efficacy scores are harmonic means of 1-minus-similarity measures.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim CiPO gives the best forgetting–utility trade-off and preserves reasoning ability. The abstract goes further, saying CiPO completely removes knowledge from CoT and answers. Their own numbers do not show complete removal: ForgetACC is about 0.32–0.34 and CoT-UA about 0.44–0.48. The ethics section says leakage may persist under adversarial prompting, but no attack is run.
record.recipe_differences: CiPO uses counterfactual reasoning and iterative preference optimization for LRMs; it is not one of the specified attack or unlearning recipes under comparison in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Forget-set ratio (1%, 5%, 10%) changes the reported outcomes; the paper also evaluates two model architectures in the real-world setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Answer-level suppression can leave the forgotten fact in the chain of thought. AnswerIDK on R1-Distill-Llama-8B drops ForgetACC to 0.0542 while CoT-UA stays 0.6354, against 0.7945 originally (Table 3). Across methods, CoT leak scores stay around 0.44–0.48 for CiPO (Tables 3–4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In reasoning models, unlearning that suppresses final answers can leave the forgotten knowledge readable in the CoT trace without any attack.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No recovery-attack evaluation; no uncertainty estimates reported for the cited table values. Real-world results use a 260-pair set, with a randomly selected 50% forget set. The paper notes that the experiments are limited to factual forgetting in QA-style settings.
record.rows_left_out: Other baseline-method entries and additional metrics in Tables 1, 3, and 4 are not included; the selected rows retain the target/original reference, CiPO, and representative GA and R2 MU comparisons. No recovery-attack results exist in the paper to extract.

untested.parts: Whether any simple attack recovers knowledge after CiPO or the baselines. Whether forget performance reaches chance (no chance level is defined).
Direction ablation, or analysis of blocking access versus deleting knowledge.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, in-context information.
CiPO is never evaluated against the attacks named in the claim.

record.verdict_notes: Changed relation from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4 and removed the reader's labels for Version A. The reader's own reasons for those labels were that no recovery attack exists, which is grounds for not testing, not for limits_scope. Every row is either own-method performance, a baseline comparison or an original-model reference, so all rows are relinked to 'none'.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge after unlearning; whether performance is at chance; attack results for each method.
Fine-tuning or relearning after unlearning, with unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
Ablating an activation direction or testing whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery through rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Whether CiPO or another method resists the attacks named in the claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It proposes an unlearning method, motivated by the incompleteness of existing methods, and tests no version of the claim. The reader's 'tests' is not supported.

tranche.reason: Methods paper reporting CiPO's own forgetting and utility against other unlearning baselines. It runs no recovery attack (no relearning, ablation, quantization or adversarial prompting), so it does not test any version. The reader's T2 is wrong.

source_check.notes: The text columns of Tables 3 and 4 are readable, but the GA/GD CoT-UA cells are merged: only one value (0.5084 in Table 3, '-' in Table 4) appears for the two rows. The abstract's 'completely removing knowledge' is not matched by the numbers: CiPO ForgetACC is 0.3178/0.3411 and CoT-UA 0.4446/0.4750. No attack is run. The ethics section says leakage may persist under adversarial prompting.

statements.correction: Table 3 (R1-Distill-Llama-8B): AnswerIDK ForgetACC 0.0542, CoT-UA 0.6354; original CoT-UA 0.7945. The 0.44-0.48 range is CiPO only: CoT-UA 0.4446 (Table 3, R1-Distill-Llama-8B) and 0.4750 (Table 4, R1-0528-Qwen3-8B). Other methods' CoT-UA on Llama: DirectIDK 0.2493, R2MU 0.4535, ReasonedIDK 0.5260, one of GA/GD 0.5084 (which row is lost in the text), AnswerIDK 0.6354. On Qwen3: DirectIDK 0.0636, ReasonedIDK 0.4193, AnswerIDK 0.8481; GA/GD, NPO and R2MU show '-' (reasoning capability absent). The text says CoT leakage persists under AnswerIDK because the CoT is not intervened on.
statements.problem: The AnswerIDK numbers are right (Table 3, R1-Distill-Llama-8B). The 0.44-0.48 range is given 'across methods', but it is CiPO's CoT-UA on the two models. Across methods CoT-UA varies widely, and AnswerIDK's own 0.6354 in the same sentence falls outside it.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CiPO on R-TOFU Forget01, Forget05, and Forget10
reader_labels.reason: Reported forgetting efficacy improves over the target model, but utility is lower and the results do not show post-unlearning attack resistance (T1-C1-AFE, T1-C1-CFE, T1-C1-MU, T1-C5-AFE, T1-C5-CFE, T1-C5-MU, T1-C10-AFE, T1-C10-CFE, T1-C10-MU).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Real-world evaluation on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B
reader_labels.reason: CiPO reduces forget accuracy and CoT leakage while retaining much of the measured utility, but forget accuracy and leakage remain nonzero; no recovery attacks are run (RW1-CiPO-F, RW1-CiPO-C, RW1-CiPO-R, RW2-CiPO-F, RW2-CiPO-C, RW2-CiPO-R).
